questions.question: Name the two forces that change a population's size, describe the four stages of the demographic cycle with their causes, and place South Africa on that journey.
questions.expected_answer: Population changes through natural growth (births minus deaths, expressed per thousand — e.g. 30 births and 12 deaths per thousand gives 18 per thousand, one comma eight percent a year) and migration (arrivals minus departures). The cycle: high stationary — high births and high deaths, numbers barely move; early expanding — death rates collapse first (piped water, immunisation, antibiotics) while births stay high, producing explosive growth; late expanding — birth rates descend too (urbanisation, girls' education, contraception, children becoming school fees), so growth decelerates; low stationary — both rates low, numbers level off or shrink without immigration. South Africa is in the later expanding stage: still young and growing, but more slowly, with internal migration toward Gauteng and the Western Cape and international migration in both directions.

questions.question: Define the nested population concepts down to the labour force, contrast the strict and expanded unemployment measures, and state the two key ratios with their denominators.
questions.expected_answer: Population (everyone) → working-age population (ages 15 to 64, those who could work) → labour force: the employed plus the strictly unemployed — no work, available for work, and actively looking. Outside the labour force sit learners, homemakers, the ill and early retirees, plus discouraged work-seekers, who want work but abandoned the search: dropped by the strict definition, restored by the expanded one — several percentage points apart in South Africa. The unemployment rate = unemployed ÷ labour force (never the population); the participation rate = labour force ÷ working-age population. South Africa's shapes: a young workforce with youth joblessness far above the overall rate, jobs stacked in the metros while former homeland regions carry heavy rates, and participation held down by discouragement.

questions.question: Explain how the labour market works as a market, what derived demand means, and how the market is partitioned by skill in South Africa.
questions.expected_answer: The roles reverse from the goods market: households supply labour, firms demand it, and the wage is the price where the curves intersect. Demand is DERIVED — a firm hires for the output workers generate, so labour demand follows the demand for goods, strengthening in booms and weakening in downswings, and slopes downward as dearer labour pushes firms to trim hiring or mechanise. Supply slopes upward: higher wages draw more people and hours into the market. A wage above equilibrium leaves willing workers unbought; the minimum wage is a price floor. The market splits by skill: scarce capabilities see demand chase limited supply (climbing salaries, persistent vacancies) while unskilled labour sees supply dwarf demand (pay squeezed toward the floor, long queues). The skills mismatch — too little of what firms hunt for, too much of what the economy absorbs weakly — is the structural core of SA unemployment, and training is the boarding pass between the gates.
